questions.stem:
If A > B ≥ C > D, which of the following is definitely true?
I. A > D  II. B > D  III. A ≥ C
questions.explanation: C is correct. Given: A > B ≥ C > D. I: A > B > D → A > D ✓. II: B ≥ C > D → B > D ✓. III: A > B ≥ C → A > C (strictly), which means A ≥ C is satisfied ✓. All three are true. Key rule: string transitivity holds across ≥ and > chains when the chain is consistent.

questions.stem: Decode: In a code, '@' means '>', '#' means '<', and '=' means '='. If P @ Q # R, which is true?

options.option_text: P > Q < R, so P and R cannot be compared definitively. All conclusions about P vs R are uncertain.

questions.explanation: D is correct. P @ Q # R decodes to P > Q < R. This tells us: (1) P is greater than Q, (2) Q is less than R. We CANNOT determine P vs R — P could be larger or smaller than R. The only safe conclusions are P > Q and Q < R. Coded inequality rule: decode first, then apply logic.

questions.stem:
Given: M ≥ N = O < P. Which conclusion is definitely TRUE?
I. M ≥ O  II. P > N  III. M > P
questions.explanation: B is correct. Given: M ≥ N = O < P. I: M ≥ N = O → M ≥ O ✓ (definite). II: N = O < P → N < P → P > N ✓ (definite). III: M ≥ O and O < P. If M = O, then M < P. If M > O, M might still be < P. Cannot conclude M > P. Only I and II are definitely true.

questions.stem: In coded inequalities: '$' means '≥', '!' means '≤', '%' means '='. If X $ Y % Z ! W, what is the relation between X and W?
questions.explanation: D is correct. Decode: X $ Y % Z ! W → X ≥ Y = Z ≤ W. Chain: X ≥ Y = Z ≤ W. We know X ≥ Z and W ≥ Z. Both X and W are on different sides of Z with no direct link — X vs W cannot be determined. Example: X=5, Z=3, W=3 → X>W; or X=3, Z=3, W=10 → X<W.

questions.stem: If A ≥ B > C ≥ D, which of the following is FALSE?
questions.explanation: C is correct. From A ≥ B > C ≥ D: the chain has a strict inequality B > C in the middle, ensuring A > D always (strictly). So A = D is IMPOSSIBLE. A > D (true), B > D (true), A ≥ C (true since A > C). The false statement is A = D.

questions.stem:
Symbols: '©' means '>'; '®' means '<'; '™' means '='; '℠' means '≥'; '℗' means '≤'.
Statement: P © Q ℠ R ® S. Conclusions: I. P > R  II. Q > S  III. P © S
questions.explanation: C is correct. Decode: P > Q ≥ R < S. I: P > Q ≥ R → P > R ✓. II: Q ≥ R < S — Q and S both sit above R but we can't compare them; e.g., Q=5, R=3, S=10 → Q<S; or Q=10, R=3, S=4 → Q>S. II is uncertain. III: P > S? P > Q ≥ R < S — same issue, P vs S is unknown. Only I is definite.

questions.stem: If J > K = L > M ≥ N, which conclusion is definitely FALSE?
questions.explanation: D is correct. From J > K = L > M ≥ N: the chain clearly shows J at the top and N at the bottom. J > N is definite. Therefore N > J is definitely false. All other options (J>M, K>N, L≥N) are provably true from the chain.

questions.stem: Statements: All A ≥ B, B > C, C = D. Conclusions: I. A > D  II. A ≥ D  III. B > D
questions.explanation: B is correct. Chain: A ≥ B > C = D. I: A ≥ B > C = D → A > D (since somewhere in the chain, B > C is strict). II: A > D satisfies A ≥ D ✓. III: B > C = D → B > D ✓. All three conclusions follow.

questions.stem: In coded form: 'δ' = '>', 'λ' = '<', 'μ' = '≥'. If E μ F δ G λ H, which is a definite conclusion?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Decode: E ≥ F > G < H. E ≥ F and F > G → E > G (since F > G and E ≥ F means E ≥ F > G). So E > G is definite. E vs H, F vs H: both uncertain because G < H on one side and E ≥ F > G on the other — the '<' in the middle blocks transitivity.

questions.stem: If X > Y ≥ Z, which among the following CANNOT be concluded?
questions.explanation: C is correct. From X > Y ≥ Z, we can conclude X > Z (and therefore X ≥ Z). Z > X directly contradicts the chain (Z ≤ Y < X). Z > X cannot be concluded and is actually false given the premises.
